message.reasoning_content:
I'm looking at Query B, the ternary inside simplify_ordering in expr.rs. The plan is a DataFrameScan, then a Sort, then a Select, with the sink as root. I think the in-memory sink keeps order because of its maintain_order setting, so the sink's in-edge and the Select's out-edge are both ordered.

I'm tracing the Select node next: the ternary has two literal branches, so the observed-order accumulation comes back empty because it's read before the mask's column order is added. That makes the Select look order-insensitive, so its input edge would be marked unordered and the sink would drop maintain_order.

The sort gets dropped once the sink's in-edge is marked unordered, so the result just follows the input order. Other variants I'm checking: a bare comparison or `then(pl.col("x"))` both report a column order and are fine, and `with_columns` is fine too because the extra column makes it an hstack that keeps input order observed. Selecting `x` alongside the flag is also fine, since `x` contributes the column order. The `head(3)` case is still open: I'm not yet sure whether the slice's in-edge stays ordered when the traversal runs top-down.

I'm checking whether the head(3) case still keeps the sort. My guess is that slice pushdown moves the slice into the Sort itself, so the Sort isn't removed because it now carries a slice.

I'm checking the head(3) case now: slice pushdown probably moves the slice into the Sort, so the Sort survives because it carries a slice. I can't run this to confirm. The cum_sum variant stays ordered at the Select's output, since it contributes an independent order, but its input edge still ends up unordered because it doesn't observe any column order.

I'm checking the remaining variants: the string-label version behaves the same, and with QueryOptFlags.none() the order-observe check is turned off, so that case is fine. The eager path doesn't produce a sort in the plan at all, and the streaming engine shares this optimizer, so it has the same problem.

I'm weighing whether the override to empty for the mask node is also part of the same mistake, since with deorder allowed the mask's order should still carry through to the output.

I'm checking the upstream logic for the ternary and binary expression case, since the observed-order result seems to depend on when the mask's order gets added. The likely fix is to compute the output's observable order after the mask is included, and to reconsider the special case that forces the mask node's output to empty.

I'm weighing whether the empty override for the mask node is harmless in the deorder case. With the output already unordered, that choice barely changes the Select's edges, but it still matches the same wrong belief about the mask's order.

I'm still weighing whether the empty override for the mask node is intentional, since it looks like the same mistaken belief about the mask's order. It probably doesn't change much here, because callers that allow deordering ignore that result anyway.

I'm checking whether the ternary's mask order should carry into the output, since the current logic drops it before the result is computed. Streaming shares this optimizer, so the same issue applies there. Next I'm looking at Query A, where the null-check conjunct gets classified as opaque.

I'm checking the classification in classify_negation for the negated is_in with nulls_equal set to true, since it treats the disallowed values as null-rejecting regardless of that flag. With nulls_equal true, a null input yields true after negation and keeps the row, so the has_value_constraint check that makes the whole predicate false looks wrong here.

I'm noticing that disallowed values don't count toward dropping nulls, unlike the other constraints, which suggests the designers kept that separate on purpose. I'm wondering whether the conflict with Null still holds, since with nulls_equal set to true the negation keeps null rows.

I'm checking the helper has_value_constraint, which counts disallowed values as conflicting with Null in resolve_deferred, and that looks like the source of the inconsistency with drops_nulls. Next I want to see every routine that reaches resolve_deferred through model_and_chain.

I'm weighing whether the wrong decision sits in classify_negation, which records the disallowed values for an is_in regardless of nulls_equal. With nulls_equal set to false, the fix in has_value_constraint would still leave the predicate intact and the runtime would return empty, so that case is fine either way.

I'm checking whether the predicate-simplification path also applies to eager DataFrame filters and the streaming engine, which would mean the same optimizer rule is involved. I still need to confirm that the eager flags include the expression simplification step.

I'm weighing two fixes for the Null-versus-disallowed conflict: either stop counting the disallowed set in `has_value_constraint`, so it matches `drops_nulls`, or change what `classify_negation` records for `is_in` when `nulls_equal` is true.

I'm weighing a narrower fix: skipping the disallowed set only when nulls_equal is false, since that is the case where the negation drops nulls. That would still catch conflicts like `a == 1 & ~a.is_in([1], nulls_equal=True)`, which hold regardless of the flag. The same question applies to the positive is_in branch, which seems to drop nulls either way.

I'm checking whether `has_value_constraint` is the right place to make the call, since it treats the disallowed set as conflicting with Null even though `drops_nulls` leaves it out on purpose. Its only caller is `resolve_deferred`, so the check should be scoped to nulls_equal cases where the negation actually drops nulls.

I'm now checking the py-polars tests for anything that shows the intended behavior of the disallowed set around nulls.
